newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Global survey launched into drug-resistant bugs.
newsitem.headline: Global survey launched into drug-resistant bugs.

text.p: Researchers have launched a global, long-term study to monitor and help control the spread of germs that are becoming resistant to antibiotics.

The programme, the early findings of which were presented to an international medical conference in Sydney this week, is the first to consider a broad range of both illnesses and drug families, Professor Ron Jones of the University of Iowa said on Thursday.
Resistance to a range of antibiotics for bacteria which cause illnesses such as pneumonia and serious skin infections is increasing around the world, particularly in the United States.
"We are paying the price for the abuse and over-use of certain drug families over the past 20 years," Jones told Reuters.
In the first eight weeks of the surveillance programme, more than 8,500 samples had been tested from the United States, South America and Canada, showing different patterns of resistance, he said.
The programme, run by the University of Iowa and the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands, would be extended to five continents and run for at least five years, Jones said.
The study from 200 sites worldwide will allow researchers to look at the frequency of diseases, and the frequency of disease resistance.
Hospitals taking part will be advised of the results to enable them to change therapies if a high degree of resistance is found.
Researchers also aim to isolate and identify unusual strains of bacteria from clusters of disease, and to arm doctors with information to control potential epidemics.
Reports of resistance have been around for more than 50 years, and drugs used to control the most intractable problems have begun to fail in some cases.
The first cases of resistance to vancomycin, the antibiotic used when others fail, to the common staph infection, staphylococcus aureus, were reported in Japan this year.
However, Jones said the outlook was not the doomsday scenario being painted some years ago.
"It's not as dismal as it might appear, there are still some older drugs and some newer drugs on the horizon that are useable," he said.
Doctors had to be more creative in their treatment, he added. "Physicians have to stop using shot-gun antibiotics, the one that looks like it's going to kill everything," he said.
"They need to think more about the way they use the drugs and become more acquainted with the characteristics of the drugs they are using."
